newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak money market rates jump.
newsitem.headline: Slovak money market rates jump.

text.p: Slovak interbank interest rates moved above 20 percent on Friday, due to a continuing money market liquidity shortage, ahead of the end of the minimum reserves requirement period (PMR) on Monday.
Traders said only short-term maturities were traded on the money market at the moment, with rates for one-day funds ranging between 19 to 22 percent.
Dealers said they did not expect rates to significantly fall in the first two weeks of July as the liquidity crunch was likely to remain on the market.

"It is now certain that (local) banking sector will not, again, meet its PMR since it will lack combined some 40 billion crowns at the end of the PMR period on Monday," said VUB Bank money market chief dealer Jaroslav Hora.
Traders said they did not expect a more significant inflow of crown funds into the market over the next two-week period from other sorces than the central bank (NBS).

"The sector will probably remain relying on the NBS funding through repo tenders as the main liquidity source over the next PMR period ," Hora said, adding he expected rates to hover at around 20 percent in the first weeks of July.

Another Bratislava-based dealer, ING Bank's Marian Tatar, said the market was unlikely to see a radical inflow of foreign funds in coming weeks despite high interest rate differential against hard currencies.
"Foreign players still appear to be believing that the Slovak crown is overvalued and expect some depreciation," Tatar said.
"They (foreign investros) are awaiting the next foreign trade figures and they are really reluctant to place any longer money in Slovakia, let's say on more than one-week maturities," he added.
The National Bank of Slovakia sharply tightened money market liquidity a month ago in order to protect the crown against speculative short-selling by foreign investors.
The money market squeeze pushed rates to record levels of above 30 percent for two weeks.

The rates have since eased, pushed down by the NBS move to resume holding regular repo tenders, but the banking sector has remained short of crown liquidity and have failed to meet PMR for five times in a row.
